p: On the anniversary Dani read her own testimony again. At fifteen she'd told the jury her father wore his red work jacket that Saturday, and that she found it wet in the washer the next morning.
The State's case came down to a man in a red jacket, seen by a neighbor across the street who never saw his face.
Joel, her supervisor, told her none of it can come near the office, not its files and not its hours.

So she climbed the stairs on Federal to Ana Brennan, the lawyer who lost her father's appeal in 2010. Ana will work with her Tuesday and Thursday nights and every other Saturday, for nothing, as long as Dani keeps her test date.
What Dani told her that first night was that a red jacket can't say which man in red the neighbor saw.
Bianca Medina. Teo's partner, and Lupe's mother.
Lupe Ruiz. Teo and Bianca's daughter. She's six, and she's never met her grandfather.
Teo Ruiz. Dani's brother. He hasn't been up to see their father in ten years.
Ana Brennan. Dani's father's lawyer now. A gray greyhound named Dicta sleeps under her desk.
Luis Ruiz. Dani's father, at Sterling. Wednesdays at seven.
Chapter two. What They Had to Believe.

Thanksgiving. Thursday, November 26. Dani did the turkey her mother's way, in at six, oven door open every twenty minutes so she could tell it what she thought of it. Teo's furnace ran all day without a click. Sage, and that burnt dust smell off the registers you only get the first real cold night. Every year she forgot it. Every year it got her in the hall.

They came at two. Bianca had a casserole she said not to judge. Teo stood in the kitchen doorway with a store pie, both hands on it like it was evidence, and Dani had to pry it off him. Lupe's crayons rattled around in a pencil box whose latch had quit in September. She was six. Anything flat was a canvas.

One picture of their father lived on the fridge, under a pizza magnet. Her fourteenth birthday, 2006, this table. Him home from the day shift in the red work jacket, laughing at whoever had the camera. In front of him on the table, a paper party hat, still flat. Lupe had never met him. She climbed on a chair for a better look and stayed up there a long time.

She drew right through dinner (holiday rules, Bianca said). Halfway through the potatoes she held it up. This is Grandpa. A man in red. Baseball cap. Grandpa doesn't wear hats, mija. Why not? You can ask him someday. Lupe chewed on that. Then she drew a purple horse underneath him, so he'd have something to ride, and put the cap on the horse.

I made his jacket red, she said. Like the picture. Is that his favorite jacket? Tía. Is the red jacket his... Teo's fork went down. Carefully, like it might go off. Lights, he said. He'd left his lights on. Out the back door, and he didn't come back in for twenty minutes. His truck was at the curb. From the window over the sink Dani could see its lights were off.

Bianca kept her eyes on the back door. He's always slept bad, she said, low, mostly to her plate. Since Halloween it's every night. Wakes up at three, goes out and sits in the truck. Won't tell me. She looked over like Dani might know. Dani didn't. Said so. Bianca nodded the way you nod at a forecast.
Could Grandpa have the drawing? Lupe asked it twice. Dani said yes before she'd thought about it.

When Teo came back in he didn't sit down. He ran the water and did the dishes, all of them, even the roasting pan she'd meant to soak till Saturday. She dried. She told him about the drawing, that Lupe wanted Grandpa to have it. He scrubbed the same corner of the pan a long time.
Put her name on it, he said. Not mine.

Friday morning it went in an envelope with the long address, the one with his number in it, and LUPE on the back in Dani's printing, into the blue box on the corner. First thing from Teo's side of the family he'd get in ten years.
Ana's Pencil: what they had to believe.

The radiator's knocking, which means the laundromat turned the boiler up, which means it's below freezing on Federal. Dicta's taken the warm end of the rug. Last time I made you find where an argument goes. Tonight we look at the road between where it starts and where it ends, because that's where arguments cheat.

Premises almost never get you all the way to a conclusion by themselves. Whatever the author needed and didn't say is an assumption. This test asks about assumptions two ways, and the two are opposites, so learn them as a pair.

The first is the necessary assumption: something the argument can't live without. Here's how you find one. Take the candidate, deny it plainly, and read the argument again. If the denial wrecks it, the assumption was necessary. If the argument limps on, it wasn't. My dryer argument: the left dryer did my load in thirty eight minutes and the right one took fifty, so the owner should put the big loads on the left. Try this one. The left dryers don't slow way down when a load is big. Deny it. Now they choke on big loads, and my one load tells the owner nothing about big ones. Wrecked. Necessary.
Deny the plain way. The denial of "all" is "not all," not "none." The denial of "some" is "none." Swing to the far opposite and everything starts to look necessary.

Here's the pair that trips people. Say an argument only needs one of the left dryers to work. Candidate: some of the left dryers work. Deny it: none of them work. Wrecked, so it's necessary. Candidate: none of the left dryers are broken. Deny it: some are broken. The argument shrugs, because one working dryer was all it needed. Too strong.

And notice what the right answer looks like here. Modest. Often it's something you'd shrug at. The trap is a choice that would help a lot but goes further than the argument needs. "Every big load in the world dries faster on the left" would help me. I don't need it.

How the exam asks it. Necessary assumption stems say the argument depends on, requires, or relies on an assumption. Deny each choice and keep the one whose denial sinks the argument. Choices stronger than the argument needs are the usual trap.

The second kind runs the other way. A sufficient assumption is one that, added to the premises, makes the conclusion follow. Not likely. Follow, with no room left. You're not asking what the argument can't live without. You're asking what would finish it.

So hunt for the new idea. Find a word in the conclusion the premises never mentioned, and build a bridge to it. Every dryer on the left was serviced in May, so the left dryers won't break down this winter. The premises talk about service. The conclusion talks about breaking down. The bridge: no dryer serviced in May will break down this winter. Add that and the conclusion has to be true.

Here strong is good. Sufficient answers are full of "all," "every," "only," and "any," because a guarantee is a strong thing. The trap runs the other direction now: a modest choice that helps without finishing.

A lot of these are conditionals. "If it was serviced in May, it won't break" says service is enough. It doesn't say service is the only way to stay running. You can run a conditional backward only if you flip both halves and deny both: if it broke, it wasn't serviced in May. That's the contrapositive, and it's always as true as the original. Flipping without denying is how most people lose these.

How the exam asks it. Sufficient assumption stems ask which choice, if assumed, allows the conclusion to be properly drawn, or which one the conclusion follows logically from. Find the idea that appears only in the conclusion, then pick the choice that connects it to the premises.

Keep the two straight with a plain case. To sit for this test you need a registration. Having one doesn't put a score on your record. Showing up and answering does that. A requirement is a floor. A guarantee is a ceiling. Most real arguments need several floors, and no one of them is enough.

Plenty of bad arguments take a requirement and treat it as a guarantee, or the other way round. You'll meet that as a flaw soon. For now, every time you read a conclusion, ask both questions. What does this need? What would be enough? They have different answers more often than you'd think. Once in a while one statement is both, an exact bridge, and it'll be right on either kind of question.

Here's a drill I make everybody do. Take any conclusion and write two lists under it in pencil. On the left goes everything the argument needs: deny each one and watch it fall. On the right goes the one sentence that would finish it. The left list is usually long and dull. The right one is usually a single line, and it usually says "only" or "every." If your right hand line is modest, it's in the wrong column.

How the exam asks it. When a flaw choice says the argument treats something required for a result as enough to bring it about, this is the mistake. Check whether the premises only show the thing was needed.
What the page lets you say.

Reading Comprehension asks the same kind of question about documents. A detail question wants what the passage states. Put your finger on the line. If you can't point to it, it isn't stated, however obvious it feels. Detail traps love to borrow the passage's words and change one: the bar becomes the lot, several becomes one.

An inference question wants what the passage lets you conclude without saying it. Still close to the text. Think of it as an assumption run backward: given what's on the page, what has to be true, or nearly? Not what's likely in the world. If a report names the people interviewed and says everyone else had left before the officers came, you can infer the others weren't interviewed at the scene. You can't infer why.

A meaning in context question names a word and asks what it means where it sits. The dictionary sense is usually the trap. Read the sentence before and the sentence after, put your own word in the slot, and only then look at the choices. A word in one report may not mean what it means in the next one.

Two habits help. When a detail answer looks right, find the exact line before you pick it. When an inference answer looks right, ask whether the passage would have to be wrong for that answer to be false. If it wouldn't, you're guessing.

One more kind tonight, because it turns up in almost every set. A function question points at a piece of the passage and asks why it's there. The author mentions the stations primarily in order to. The second paragraph serves to. The stem doesn't want what the piece says. It wants the job it does: gives an example, answers an objection, sets up a contrast, gives ground before the turn. Work one with me. A passage argues that a city's first underground railway was built for freight, not people. Halfway through it says the early stations had no benches. Why mention benches? Not to tell you about furniture. It's evidence for the freight claim. Nobody plans seats for coal. So the function of that sentence is to support the main claim with a detail of the design.

The trap answers hand the detail back to you. To describe the stations is true and useless. Another trap gives the piece a bigger job than it has: to prove the line never carried a passenger, when it only made freight likelier. So read the sentence before and the sentence after, say what the piece serves to do with your own verb, support, illustrate, concede, contrast, and only then look at the choices. Now a variation. Same passage, but the benches line comes right after critics point out that the railway later carried millions of riders. Now the benches line serves to answer the critics. The riders came later, and the design came first. Same sentence, different job, because a sentence's job depends on what's around it.

How the exam asks it. Detail stems start "according to the passage." Inference stems say "it can be inferred," "suggests," or "most strongly supports." Meaning stems ask what a word or phrase most nearly means as used in the passage. Function stems ask why the author mentions something, or what a part serves to do. Go back to the line every time.

The denial test only works if you deny the right thing. Most people who miss assumption questions know the test cold and swing too far when they use it. So here's how to deny a choice, piece by piece, and two worked questions.

Deny the smallest amount. All the dryers work becomes at least one dryer doesn't. Some dryer works becomes no dryer works. Most of the regulars come on Saturdays becomes half or fewer do. Always becomes sometimes not. At least two becomes one or none. Each time, ask what's the least that has to go wrong for the choice to be false. That least is the denial.

Choices with two parts need care. Deny an and, and you only have to break one half. The new dryers are faster and cheaper becomes they aren't faster, or they aren't cheaper. Deny an or, and you have to break both. The machines are faster or cheaper becomes they're neither. That matters here. A choice that needs two things to be true is easy to deny, since one broken half is enough, so it's necessary only if each half is. A choice that offers two ways out is hard to deny, since both have to break, and that's why a modest either or is so often the necessary one.

Choices that are rules get denied the way any rule does. If a machine is new, it's faster becomes there's a new machine that isn't faster. One case. You don't need every new machine to be slow. You need one that breaks the rule.

Work one. A diner owner says: our new grill cooks a burger in four minutes instead of seven, so we'll be able to serve more customers at lunch. The question asks for an assumption the argument requires. One choice says cooking time is what limits how many customers can be served at lunch. Deny it: something else sets the limit, say the one cook who assembles every plate. Then a faster grill just makes burgers wait at the counter, and lunch doesn't get any faster. Wrecked. Necessary. Another choice says most customers at lunch order burgers. Deny it: half or fewer do. The argument limps a little and still stands, since the burger orders still get out faster. Not necessary. A third says the new grill will never break down. Deny it: it'll break down at least once. The argument doesn't care. Too strong, and the far swing is what makes it feel important.

Work one where the argument is a rule. A clerk says: anyone who files before Friday gets a reply within a week, and Nell filed Thursday, so she'll hear back by next Thursday. That one's tight already. Now change it so it has a hole. Anyone who files before Friday at the front desk gets a reply within a week. Nell filed Thursday, so she'll hear back by next Thursday. What does it need? That Nell filed at the front desk. Deny it, she mailed it in, and the rule never reaches her. The hole in a conditional argument is almost always a condition the case was never shown to meet.

Sufficient questions go the other way, and arrows make them quick. Write the premise as an arrow and the conclusion as an arrow, then find the missing link. The premise: filed before Friday at the front desk, then a reply within a week. The conclusion: filed before Friday, then a reply within a week. The link that finishes it: filed before Friday, then filed at the front desk. Odd as a fact, perfect as a bridge. Add it and the conclusion can't fail. Most sufficient questions have that shape somewhere, even when the words hide it: the conclusion's new idea at one end, the premises' idea at the other, and the answer is the plank between them.

When you miss one of these, check two things first. Did you deny the choice too hard? And did you mix up the two questions, keeping a modest choice that helps when the stem wanted the one that guarantees? Those two cover most misses on assumption questions.

How the exam asks it. Necessary stems say the argument depends on the assumption that, requires the assumption that, or ask for an assumption required by the argument. Deny each choice by the smallest amount, then reread the argument. Sufficient stems use if assumed and properly drawn. Write premise and conclusion as arrows and find the plank between them.
Needed or enough, side by side.

Same argument, both questions, so you can hear the difference in the answers. A bakery owner says: our rye sold out by noon every day last week, so if we bake twice as much rye this week, we'll sell twice as much.

Necessary first. What can't the argument live without? That the people who wanted rye last week didn't all get it. Deny it: everybody who wanted rye got some before it ran out, and the sellout just means the batch was the right size. Then twice the rye sits on the shelf. Wrecked. Necessary. Notice how modest it is. It doesn't say demand will double. It only says there was demand nobody met.

Sufficient next. What would finish it? Something like: every week, the bakery can sell all the rye it bakes. Strong, a little silly, and if it's true the conclusion follows. That's what sufficient answers look like. They'd make you raise an eyebrow in real life, and they close the gap all the way.

Now swap them and watch each one fail the other test. Put the sufficient answer on the necessary question: deny it, there's some week the bakery can't sell all it bakes. Does the argument fall? No. This week could still go fine. So it's not necessary. Put the necessary answer on the sufficient question: there was demand nobody met last week. Does that guarantee twice the sales? No. The unmet demand might be ten loaves. So it's not sufficient. One argument, two questions, two different right answers, and each one is the other's trap.

How the exam asks it. When you can't tell whether a choice is necessary or sufficient, run both tests. Deny it to check necessary. Add it to the premises to check sufficient. The stem tells you which test counts.

Tuesday, December 1, Ana had moved one wall of banker's boxes, and behind them was a whiteboard nobody had written on in years. A phone number in one corner had faded to a blue ghost. Ana wiped it off with her sleeve.

Dani had brought the last of the turkey up the stairs in foil. Ana looked at it longer than she'd looked at the police report. Nobody brings me food, she said. She ate all of it standing at the whiteboard and didn't say thank you, and Dicta watched every bite.
Across the top, in small square capitals, she wrote the sentence from the first night: THE MAN CONSUELO BACA SAW WAS LUIS RUIZ. Under it she drew a line, a long one, all the way across.
Under the line goes everything they never said and couldn't do without, she said. Start with the jacket. Consuelo saw red. He wore red. What did they have to believe for red to point at him?
Dani thought about a refinery crew in matching jackets, and a city full of people who'd come for the Red Sox. On the rug Dicta sighed, like she'd heard this one before.
A. "That he'd been angry enough at Travis to go back out to the lot looking for him."
B. "That he was the only man in a red jacket anywhere near that lot that whole night."
C. "That red jackets weren't so common around there that red could mean anybody."
D. "That Travis Hensley had noticed his jacket during the shoving inside the bar."

1. RED WASN'T COMMON, in those square capitals, under the line. Ana caps the marker. Deny it. Say red's everywhere that night. What's their jacket worth now? Nothing. It's a color. Mm hm. Dani starts in on the World Series, the Boston people, the crew. Up comes the pencil. Evidence. Later. Tonight we only write what they needed.

That's the one. Pencil down. Necessary assumption. Run the denial: red jackets all over that lot. Now a man in red could be any of a dozen guys, and the name falls off. And look how little it claims. Not the only man in red. Red wasn't everywhere, that's all.
Ana tapped the board with the eraser end. Number two. The lab found Travis Hensley's blood on the cuff. Their closing says the blood says he did it. Did what? Where?

Dani knew this part. Her father had told the police he never touched anyone, not inside and not outside. The State had leaned on that all week at trial. A man with nothing to hide doesn't lie about a fight.
For blood on a cuff to put him in the lot, Ana said, what did they have to believe about it?
A. "That Travis was already bleeding before Consuelo ever saw him get hit."
B. "That he washed the jacket after he'd seen the blood on the cuff that night."
C. "That none of Travis's blood got on his cuff, not even in the fight inside the bar."
D. "That the blood didn't all get on him during the shoving inside the bar."

2. SOME OF THE BLOOD CAME FROM THE ATTACK, NOT THE BAR. Ana steps back from it. Here's what your father did to himself. If he'd told them, sure, we shoved, he scratched me, then the cuff is bar blood and number two is just a fight. He told them he never touched the man. Because he didn't. Ana looks at her. Then where'd the blood come from? Dani doesn't have an answer, and Ana doesn't wait for one.

Right. Now say why. Necessary assumption. Deny it: all of the blood got there during the fight inside. Then the cuff shows a bar fight and nothing about the lot. The word "all" matters. Some blood from inside and some from outside still works for the State.

Thursday the boxes were on Ana's desk, two of them, ABRAMS, RUIZ 07CR on the ends in black marker. They'd come out of storage that week addressed to Ana, because Ana was his lawyer now and Dani wasn't. Phil Abrams had died in 2019. His handwriting was all over everything, slanted and fast.
Nothing in the first box had ever been in her basement. Her mother had kept the transcript. She hadn't had any way to keep this.
The police report was near the top, three pages stapled at the corner. Ana read it and passed it across without a word.

Commerce City Police Department, offense report, Sunday, October 28, 2007, a quarter past two in the morning. Reporting officer: D. Archuleta. Dispatched at eleven seventeen Saturday night to the rear lot of the Night Owl Tap, Highway 2, on a report of an assault. Victim Travis Hensley, 31, found on his back at the curb, unresponsive, bleeding from the head. Transported by ambulance at eleven thirty one. Hospital reports victim pronounced dead at one forty in the morning. Witness Consuelo Baca, residing across the street, states that at about a quarter past eleven she observed from her kitchen window a male in a red jacket strike the victim with an unknown object. Subject fled on foot northbound. Witness did not see the subject's face. Bartender Ronald Galvan states the victim and a regular customer, Luis Ruiz, were in a shoving fight inside the bar at about ten twenty five, and that he separated them. Galvan states Ruiz left the bar at about a quarter to eleven. Galvan states Ruiz wore a red Platte Valley work jacket, and that several men from the refinery wore the same jacket in the bar during the game. Victim's sister, Shannon Hensley, by phone, states the victim called her at four minutes after eleven and said, "The guy from the bar is still out here. Come get me." Remaining patrons had left before officers arrived. Names not obtained. Subject not located. Referred to Investigations, Detective G. Vigil.
Start with the clock, Ana said. What does this say about when your father left? Says. Not means.
A. Luis got in his truck and drove out of the lot at about a quarter to eleven.
B. Luis was still out in the back lot at four minutes after eleven that night.
C. Luis told the officer himself that he'd gone home by a quarter to eleven.
D. The bartender says Luis walked out of the bar at about a quarter to eleven.

The bar, Ana says. Not the lot. Not the neighborhood. Galvan watched him go out a door. Anything after that door, this report doesn't know. Dani underlines the word bar so hard the pencil goes through.

Good. That's how you read it. Specific detail. Put your finger on the line: Galvan states Ruiz left the bar at about a quarter to eleven. That's what it says, at that size. Where he went after the door isn't stated anywhere on the page.
Ana let her sit with it. Downstairs the dryers had started on the evening loads, a low roll through the floor.

Then: Now the jacket. Same rule. What does the report say about it? Dani read the Galvan paragraph again, slower. Galvan states Ruiz wore a red Platte Valley work jacket, and that several men from the refinery wore the same jacket in the bar during the game. She'd read a hundred police reports at work. She'd never read one about her own kitchen.
A. Galvan says Luis wore a red Platte Valley jacket, as did several refinery men.
B. Consuelo told the officer the jacket said Platte Valley, in letters across the back.
C. Galvan says Luis wore a red jacket just like the one Consuelo saw in the lot.
D. The officer saw Travis Hensley's blood on the cuff of the red jacket Luis wore.

Several, Ana says. On the first night of the case, in the first report anybody wrote. Phil had this. She doesn't say anything else about Phil. Dani reads the word again. Several. It was there before anyone had a name.

That's the one. Pencil down. Specific detail. The line says Ruiz wore a red Platte Valley work jacket and that several men from the refinery wore the same jacket in the bar. Say both halves, because the second half is the one that matters.

Ana read the sister's line out loud, flat. 'The guy from the bar is still out here. Come get me.' She put the page down. At trial they put in her phone records and put Shannon on the stand to say those words. What job was that line doing for them?
Dani had seen Shannon Hensley once, in 2008, in the hallway outside the courtroom. Shannon had looked right at her. Dani had been fifteen and had looked at the floor.
A. It backs a middle step: that the man from the fight was still there after a quarter to eleven.
B. It's background, there to show the jury that Travis was frightened before he was attacked.
C. It's a premise that goes straight to the conclusion that Luis was the one who hit Travis.
D. It's the main conclusion, and everything else in the case is there to support that call.

Ana nods. Galvan sends him out the door at 10:45. Their case needs him back in the lot at 11:15. This call sits in the middle and holds the two together. She draws it on the board, a small box between two bigger ones. Take it out and there's half an hour with nobody in it.

Right. Now say why. Role of a statement. The call supports an intermediate claim, that the man from the bar fight was still near the lot after he left the bar, and that claim supports the identification. Arrows in and out of a middle box: that's the job.
Decision six. The guy from the bar.
So for that middle box, Ana said, what did they have to believe about four words? The guy from the bar.

Dani tried to picture the Night Owl at 10:30 on a World Series night. Couldn't. Never been inside. At 10:30 that night she'd been fifteen, on somebody's floor in Thornton, with birthday cake and a borrowed sleeping bag that smelled like a dog.
A. "That Shannon called the police the minute she got off the phone with her brother."
B. "That Travis hadn't had any more to drink than the people around him that night."
C. "That when Travis said 'the guy from the bar' he meant the man he'd fought."
D. "That Luis was the only man in the whole bar Travis had words with that night."
Ana writes it, quote marks and all. 3. "THE GUY FROM THE BAR" WAS LUIS. Dani stares at it. It was a bar full of guys. Put that in your pocket, Ana says. You'll want it later.

Good. That's how you read it. Necessary assumption. Deny it, say Travis meant somebody else from the bar, and the call says nothing about Luis. The middle box is empty. The phrase only helps the State if it points at the man from the fight.

Saturday, December 5, the first of Ana's every other Saturdays. Ana had sorted Phil's loose notes into a pile on the corner of the desk, under a stapler, and Dani read them while Ana was on the phone with a court clerk about something else.

Phil Abrams's notes, loose in the front of box one. March 12, 2008. Galvan at prelim. Says client swung first. Get the bar tab. Who else was there? April 2, 2008. Client won't discuss the fight. Says nothing happened. May 14, 2008. Jail visit. Client says no stops. Ask again re daughter. May 20, 2008. Eyewitness expert? No funds. Ask again. June 3, 2008. Daughter tomorrow. Short cross. Be kind.
Re daughter. Her, then, twice on one page. The first was lawyer shorthand she couldn't read. The second one she could.
Be kind. Dani read that one twice. She remembered his voice, asking if she was okay to keep going, and she remembered thinking at fifteen that he was on the wrong side to be asking.
Ana hung up. Back to the report. Who did they talk to that night? And what does that tell you about who they didn't?
A. Galvan was the only person who saw the two men shoving each other in the bar.
B. Luis was questioned at the scene by the officers before he went home that night.
C. The officers didn't question the other customers because they figured they knew nothing.
D. The officers didn't question a single one of the bar's customers at the scene.

Remaining patrons had left. Names not obtained, Ana reads. A bar full of men on a World Series night, and the first report has one of them. Dani looks at the note on the stapler pile. Get the bar tab. Who else was there? Phil had asked. There's nothing in the box that says anybody answered.

That's the one. Pencil down. Inference. The report lists the bartender, the neighbor and the sister by phone. Travis was unresponsive, Galvan has Luis gone at 10:45, and the remaining patrons had left with names not obtained. So no customer was questioned at the scene. The report doesn't say so in those words, but it can't mean anything else.
The last line of the report was short. Subject not located. Referred to Investigations, Detective G. Vigil.
Dani had read Gene Vigil's later reports in the trial exhibits. In those, a few days on, "the subject" was her father, every time, with his date of birth after it.
What does subject mean, Ana said, right there, in that sentence, at two in the morning?
A. The topic of the report itself, the assault in the Night Owl's back lot.
B. The man in the red jacket Consuelo saw, whoever he turned out to be.
C. Any suspect in the case, which by Sunday afternoon was her father.
D. Travis Hensley, the man the whole report was written about that night.

The man Consuelo saw, Dani says, whoever he turned out to be. Whoever he was, Ana says. Subject fled on foot. Subject not located. Same man, the one in Consuelo's paragraph. Somewhere between this page and the next one, they wrote a name into that word. Dani reads the line again. On foot.

Right. Now say why. Meaning in context. The report uses "subject" first right after Consuelo's account, for the man who fled on foot, and the last line uses it the same way. In this document it means that unknown man.
Last one, Ana said. Galvan has him out the door at 10:45. Consuelo has a man in red at 11:15. That's half an hour. What did they need to believe to cover it?

Dani looked at the board. Three lines under the long one now. She thought about her father's truck, the old Ford with the bench seat, and how she'd never once in her life seen him walk anywhere he could drive.
A. "That Galvan was wrong, and he really left the bar later than 10:45."
B. "That he drove home first and then came back to the lot to find Travis."
C. "That he was somewhere near that lot when Consuelo looked out her window."
D. "That his truck was still sitting in that lot at a quarter past eleven."

4. NEAR THE LOT AT 11:15. Ana underlines it twice. Nobody ever proved that. They didn't think they had to. Dani reads the report again: subject fled on foot. She thinks about a man with a truck running north on foot. She doesn't say it. Ana looks at her face. Not tonight, Ana says.

Good. That's how you read it. Necessary assumption. Deny it: he wasn't anywhere near the lot at 11:15. Then he can't be the man Consuelo saw, and everything above the line falls. It's modest, too. It doesn't say how he got there, or whether he stayed or came back. Only that he was there.

Wednesday, December 9, seven, basement stairs. Recording first. Same lady, same speech about where the call's from, which Dani could do in her sleep and sometimes did. Then her father, not even a hello. I got a man on a purple horse.

That's you. I figured. Never been on a horse in my life. Smiling. She could hear it. Horse has a hat on. She wanted you in one. So the horse gets it. He laughed. The real one, from the chest, that she hadn't heard since July. Smart girl. What's she like, mija? Give me one thing.

She gave him three. Lupe hums when she draws, one note mostly, and gets mad if you notice. She has Teo's eyebrows. Not like them. His. She'd climbed on a chair to see his picture. Nothing on the line for a while but hiss. Then, quieter: Your brother? No, Pa. No okay this time. He let the hiss have it.

He asked about the lawyer. Brennan, he said. I remember that name. She had my appeal. A pause, long enough for the hiss. She lost. Wrote me two pages after, by hand. Most of them don't write. Then fast, a thing he'd been carrying since Sunday: So she shows them the jacket's no good. Then they let me out. That's how it goes?
A. "If the jacket's no good, the whole case is no good. That's how it goes, Pa."
B. "If the jacket goes and nothing else can point at you without it, then yes."
C. "If the jury had heard you tell it yourself, Pa, it would've gone the other way."
D. "I'm going to get you out of there, Pa. However long it takes. I promise."
Quiet. Then: You sound like her already. I've been sitting in her office. Good. Knight out, his move. She gives him hers. Nobody says promise.

That's the one. Pencil down. Sufficient assumption. This names what would actually be enough. Losing the jacket alone isn't. Losing the jacket, with nothing else able to identify him on its own, is the kind of thing that would be enough. Bridge the gap all the way, and say nothing more than that.

Thursday, December 10, Ana had drawn a second column on the whiteboard, to the right of the four lines. At the top of the left one she'd written NEEDED. At the top of the right one, ENOUGH. The right one was empty.
Most people hand me tonight's answer on Tuesday, and I tell them it's too strong, she said. You didn't. Let's see if you can find it now.
One sentence. If it were true, their conclusion would follow from what they had. Not probably. Follow. What is it?
A. "That Consuelo Baca told the officer and the jury the truth, every word."
B. "That he was the only man in a red jacket anywhere near that lot at 11:15."
C. "That he had a reason to go after Travis again after their fight in the bar."
D. "That red jackets weren't so common around there that red could mean anybody."

Ana writes it under ENOUGH. Consuelo saw a man in red near the lot. Your father was the only man in red near the lot. Then the man was your father. Nothing left to argue. She taps the column. They never proved it. They never even said it. They let the jury feel it.

Right. Now say why. Sufficient assumption. Add it to the premises and the conclusion is guaranteed: the man in red was the only man in red, so it was Luis. It's stronger than anything the State needed, which is fine here. A sufficient assumption is allowed to be strong.

Ana let her take the dispatch folder home. That's Phil's original. Not a copy. Ana held it a second before she let go. Bring it back Tuesday. Read it at your table, not on the bus. It went in her bag next to the prep book. The January test was five weeks out. She'd done six practice questions all week.

At home she didn't open the folder. She sat at the kitchen table under the photo on the fridge and drew two columns on an envelope. NEEDED. ENOUGH. Then she did what she'd never done in nineteen years. She wrote her own doubt across the top, the way you'd write the State's conclusion, so she could look at it. Maybe he did it.
NEEDED was easy. She'd been living in it. What would be ENOUGH? What one thing, if she knew it was true, would end it?
A. That he was somewhere else at a quarter past eleven, anywhere but that lot.
B. That Teo really was at Abuela's that whole night, like Pa always tells it.
C. That the State's argument doesn't hold up against him, start to finish.
D. That he's never lied to me about anything that really mattered. Not once.

She writes it under ENOUGH. Somewhere else at 11:15. If that's true, he's not the man in the lot, and there's nothing left to doubt. Then she looks at it for a long time, because nobody has ever said where. He says home. Home alone. She was in Thornton. Nobody was home to see him come in.

Good. That's how you read it. Sufficient assumption. If Luis was somewhere else at 11:15, he couldn't be the man Consuelo saw, and "he didn't do it" follows. That's a bridge that closes the gap all the way, which is what a sufficient assumption does.

She didn't open the folder until after eleven. Phil Abrams had put a tab on it that said 911 in his slanted capitals, and inside were a few pages of gray printout, faint, the kind that came off a printer nobody had changed the ribbon on.
On the counter her phone showed the call from Wednesday, nineteen minutes. He'd asked one thing about the case and eleven about Lupe. She'd counted.
Ana had said one thing as she'd walked her to the stairs. You write down the gap before you argue with it. Keep doing that. It's the whole job.

Most of the printout was codes. Units assigned, units on the way, a time stamp every line. On the second page somebody, Phil probably, had run a yellow highlighter across one entry, and the yellow stopped partway, right at the end of the words everyone in the case already knew: male, red jacket. The rest of the line was there. It had always been there. Nobody had colored it in.

Dispatch log, Saturday, October 27, 2007, page two. Eleven seventeen and thirty eight seconds: 911 call received. The caller, C. Baca, lives across from the rear lot of the Night Owl Tap, on Highway 2. Eleven seventeen and fifty two seconds: the caller says a male, red jacket, ball cap, struck the victim with an unknown object, and the subject fled on foot. Eleven eighteen and twenty seconds: the victim is down at the curb, not moving. Medical requested. Eleven eighteen and forty one seconds: unit two fourteen en route.
She read it again, because that was the rule. Go back and find the line. Don't answer from memory.
The envelope was still by her elbow. MAYBE HE DID IT, in her own capitals. A cap didn't put him anywhere. She knew exactly what Ana would say. She didn't cross anything out.

Then she looked up at the fridge. Her fourteenth birthday. Her father in the red jacket, laughing, and on the table in front of him the paper hat her mother had tried to put on him and he'd taken right back off.

Every picture she owned. Every Wednesday for nineteen years, when she closed her eyes on the basement stairs and saw him. Bareheaded. Not at the refinery, not at Coors Field, not at the lake in August with the sun on him. Hats make me look like my brother, he used to say, and her mother laughed every single time.
